A fictional town is establishing a shared workshop with a small number of machines and many residents who want to use them. It wants newcomers to get a fair chance, experienced users to complete demanding projects, few unused bookings, and rules that residents can understand and challenge. The town does not know how demand or strategic booking will change once the rules are introduced. Design a workable allocation arrangement and explain why it should remain fair and useful as people respond to it.

END PROBLEM

In detail: divide each machine's bookable time into equal blocks each week. Reserve 60% of blocks for the Open Pool and 40% for the Project Pool, with the split published and adjustable only within a pre-announced range after review. The Open Pool is allocated by lottery: every resident gets one base ticket per block; a newcomer gets a one-time guaranteed first-use token and, for the first three bookings, one extra ticket; anyone who has not used the workshop in 90 days gets one extra ticket. To avoid repeated losses for urgent or schedule-constrained residents, 10% of Open Pool blocks are reserved for urgent/essential use and recurring schedule windows, allocated by lottery among eligible applicants. If fewer eligible residents claim the reserved blocks than are reserved, every unclaimed reserved block returns immediately to the general Open Pool draw for that block or, if the general draw has already occurred, to the standby instant-fill queue; no reserved block is held unused. The reserve is capped at 10% of Open Pool blocks and can be adjusted only between 5% and 15% after public review, with a rollback trigger if it raises non-urgent wait times or unused bookings beyond pre-announced bounds. Any resident who loses two consecutive Open Pool draws receives one priority ticket in the next draw. The Project Pool is for projects needing at least three blocks in a month. Applicants submit a one-page public plan, requested blocks, and milestones. A rotating resident-staff panel scores plans using a published rubric with objective indicators and anchors: feasibility (materials, skills, certification, time estimate), public benefit (residents served, open output, shared repair, teaching), and readiness (confirmed materials, training, prior milestones). Panel decisions must give written rubric-linked reasons, and priority expires after the project window and is not transferable. Experienced users can receive contiguous blocks, but unused Project Pool blocks are progressively released: milestone check and tentative release to the priority waitlist at 72 hours, firm release to the Open Pool at 24 hours, and a standby instant-fill queue at start; cancellations automatically promote the next waitlisted resident. A fictional town is establishing a shared workshop with a small number of machines and many residents who want to use them. It wants newcomers to get a fair chance, experienced users to complete demanding projects, few unused bookings, and rules that residents can understand and challenge. The town does not know how demand or strategic booking will change once the rules are introduced. Design a workable allocation arrangement and explain why it should remain fair and useful as people respond to it.
